Year 8 Enquiry • 1783–1914

The Second British Empire (1783–1914)

Naval Hegemony, De-industrialisation, The 1857 Rebellion & The Scramble for Africa
Visual Decoding • 4 Core Features Walter Crane (1886)

Published for Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee, Walter Crane illustrated British global dominion, placing Britannia enthroned atop the world surrounded by colonial subjects:

1. Global Sovereignty:
Britannia enthroned with trident and shield, commanding world oceans with the British lion.
2. Imperial Red Shading:
Every colony tinted red on Mercator projection, exaggerating British worldwide territory.
3. Naval Sea Lanes:
Global steam trade routes guarded by Royal Navy ironclads, asserting industrial hegemony.
4. Subordinated Peoples:
Colonial subjects depicted bearing commodities, legitimising racial hierarchy as natural order.
Red Shading
Dominance on global Mercator maps.
Britannia’s Trident
Naval supremacy under Two-Power Standard.
Labouring Subjects
Moral justification for resource extraction.
Disciplinary Significance: In late 19th-century Britain, popular cartography transformed colonial conquest into a glorious imperial federation, hiding the violent realities of exploitation behind colourful patriotic propaganda.
Disciplinary Hinge Question: Evaluation
Does this map celebrate a cooperative global commonwealth of mutual progress, or does it disguise a coercive racial empire sustained by naval dominance and economic extraction?
Primary Visual Evidence: Imperial Federation: Map of the World Showing the Extent of the British Empire in 1886 • Walter Crane BRITISH LIBRARY ARCHIVE • MAPS 957.(46.)
Course Specification • Key Enquiry Sequence Learnt Revised
Enquiry 1: Engines of Empire: Mercantilism, Naval Hegemony & Portsmouth Dockyard (1783–1889)
How was the British Empire built and sustained through maritime industrial power?
Enquiry 2: The De-industrialisation of India: The Company & Handloom Crisis (1700–1850)
How did British corporate rule transform India from the world’s textile workshop into a captive market?
Enquiry 3: The 1857 Indian Rebellion: Sepoy Grievance, Rani Lakshmibai & The Raj (1848–1858)
Was the 1857 Indian Rebellion a limited military mutiny or a war for national liberation?
Enquiry 4: The Scramble for Africa & Imperial Ideology: Maxim Guns & Plunder (1884–1920)
Why did European powers partition Africa after 1884, and was it a civilising mission or armed resource theft?
Enquiry 5: The Imperial Verdict: Workshop of the World or Age of Exploitation? (1851–1901)
Did the British Empire bring global modernisation and order, or economic exploitation and devastation?
Between 1783 and 1914, Britain ruled a quarter of the globe through industrial manufacturing, naval supremacy, and colonial extraction. 1/16
ENQUIRY 1 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • THE SECOND BRITISH EMPIRE (1783–1914)

How was the British Empire built and sustained through maritime industrial power?

Audio • Quiz
Stage 1 1783–1805 • How did Navigation Acts enrich British ports through colonial trade?
Stage 2 1805–1815 • How did Admiral Nelson’s tactics win sea control at Trafalgar in 1805?
Stage 3 1815–1850 • Why was Portsmouth Royal Dockyard vital to Britain’s naval power?
Stage 4 1860 • How did HMS Warrior make wooden battleships outdated in 1860?
Stage 5 1889 • What did the 1889 Two-Power Standard require from the Royal Navy?
2/16 Portsmouth Royal Dockyard was the industrial beating heart of the British Empire, building the ironclads that commanded the oceans.

ENQUIRY 2 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • THE SECOND BRITISH EMPIRE (1783–1914)

How did British corporate rule transform India from the world’s textile workshop into a captive market?

Audio • Quiz
Stage 1 1650–1700 • How did Mughal India become the world’s leading cloth workshop?
Stage 2 1700–1721 • Why did Parliament pass the 1700 and 1721 Calico Acts against Indian cloth?
Stage 3 August 1765 • How did the 1765 Diwani let the Company buy Indian silk without silver?
Stage 4 1800–1830 • How did Lancashire mills and 70% border taxes ruin Indian weavers?
Stage 5 1834–1850 • How did collapsing cloth exports affect weaving towns like Dhaka by 1834?
4/16 Before British rule, India produced 25% of the world’s manufactured goods; by 1947, colonial de-industrialisation reduced that share to under 2%.

ENQUIRY 4 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • THE SECOND BRITISH EMPIRE (1783–1914)

Why did European powers partition Africa after 1884, and was it a civilising mission or armed resource theft?

Audio • Quiz
Stage 1 1884–1885 • Why did fourteen Western nations meet in Berlin in 1884 with no Africans?
Stage 2 1884 • How did the rule of Effective Occupation speed up inland conquest?
Stage 3 1884–1898 • How did quinine medicine and Maxim guns enable conquest in Africa?
Stage 4 1899 • How did Rudyard Kipling’s 1899 poem try to justify overseas conquest?
Stage 5 1920 • How did King Leopold II’s rubber quotas cause terror across the Congo?
10/16 Hilaire Belloc captured the brutal technological reality of the Scramble: "Whatever happens, we have got / The Maxim Gun, and they have not."

ENQUIRY 5 • LESSON NOTEBOOK YEAR 8 • THE SECOND BRITISH EMPIRE (1783–1914)

Did the British Empire bring global modernisation and order, or economic exploitation and devastation?

Audio • Quiz
Stage 1 1851 • What did the 1851 Great Exhibition and Koh-i-Noor diamond show?
Stage 2 1870–1900 • Why did British engineers build 25,000 miles of railways across India?
Stage 3 1876–1900 • Why did ten million Indians starve while grain was shipped to Britain?
Stage 4 1901 • What did Dadabhai Naoroji’s "Drain of Wealth" argument prove in 1867?

12/16 Dadabhai Naoroji, Britain’s first Indian MP, used official British records to prove that colonial taxation bled India of industrial capital.

Key Stage 3 History Assessment Pathways • Level Descriptors & Criteria Years 7–9 Standards
Emerging • 35%
Identifies key names, dates, and terms; describes what happened using simple statements and structured writing frames.
Emerging+ • 50%
Describes reasons why events occurred; begins to explain causes and consequences supported by basic historical facts.
Expected • 65%
Constructs structured paragraphs explaining multiple causes and consequences; substantiates arguments with precise historical dates, key terms, and named figures.
Expected+ • 80%
Weighs competing factors and perspectives; explains why certain causes were more decisive than others using detailed, accurate evidence across the unit.
Greater Depth • 90%
Crafts sustained, analytically rigorous arguments reaching a substantiated historical judgement; masterfully synthesizes evidence across the unit to evaluate complex turning points and long-term significance.
